title: Irretrievable breakdown of marriage - why it's still not a statutory ground
p1:
A marriage can be over in every practical sense… yet the law may still refuse to call it finished.

Many people assume that when two spouses have completely lost their relationship, divorce should automatically follow. But there is a surprising legal gap.
p2:
The common belief is that 'irretrievable breakdown of marriage' is already a recognised ground for divorce everywhere. In reality, in some legal systems it is not a statutory ground, meaning it is not directly written into the law as a reason to end a marriage.

The idea behind this is that lawmakers often worry about making divorce too easy and want safeguards to protect vulnerable spouses or prevent abandonment of responsibilities.
p3:
Irretrievable breakdown simply means the marriage has reached a point where reconciliation is no longer realistic. While courts may consider facts showing a relationship has collapsed, the law may still require parties to fit within existing legal grounds.

The bigger lesson: social reality and legal rules do not always change at the same speed.
conclusion: Do you think irretrievable breakdown should become a direct statutory ground for divorce, or should the law continue to place limits on ending a marriage?
